naran-town.story: In the upper Kaghan Valley of Mansehra District, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan, you’ll come upon Naran, a town and tourist destination sitting at an altitude of 2,409 meters. Around it lies an Alpine landscape where forests and meadows dominate, paired with a subarctic climate of significant summer rainfall and heavy winter snowfall. Through many days the weather remains cloudy, and even so, winters often bring temperatures below 0 °C while summers rarely exceed 15 °C. For your visit, know that Naran stays busy during the tourism season, which starts in spring and stretches well into the fall.
naran-town.name: Naran

lake-saiful-muluk.story: Traveller, at the northern end of the Kaghan Valley, near Naran in Saiful Muluk National Park, a mountainous lake waits in northern Pakistan: Lake Saiful Muluk. It is named after a legendary prince from the folk tale Saiful Muluk, later put into poem form by the Sufi poet Mian Muhammad Bakhsh, and at 3,224 m above sea level it lies above the tree line as one of the highest lakes in Pakistan. About 9 kilometres north of Naran in the Mansehra District of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, it sits near Malika Parbat, the highest peak in the valley, accessible from Naran in summer though winter access is limited by heavy snowfall and landslides that threaten to cut it off. Formed by glacial moraines that blocked a stream, it gathered from melting water after rising temperatures and receding glaciers left a depression in the Kaghan Valley, formed in the greater Pleistocene Period dating back almost 300,000 years when the area was covered with ice.
lake-saiful-muluk.name: Lake Saiful Muluk

ansoo-lake.story: Traveller, let Ansoo Lake—translated as Teardrop Lake—draw you into the Kaghan Valley of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, where this tear-shaped body of water rests in Pakistan’s Mansehra District. At 4,126 metres (13,537 ft) above sea level, it is one of the highest lakes in the Himalayan Range and lies in proximity to Malika Parbat, the tallest peak in the Kaghan Valley. It was stumbled upon in 1993 by Pakistan Air Force pilots flying at a relatively low altitude over the region. As growing tourism strains the path to the lake and its natural surroundings, its ecological fragility is revealed.
ansoo-lake.name: Ansoo Lake

malika-parbat.story: Traveller, Malika Parbat—the Queen of the Mountains—is the highest peak in the Kaghan Valley and the Hazara region of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan, at 5,290 metres. It lies about 6 kilometres south of Lake Saiful Muluk, near Ansoo Lake, and towers in the background near that popular tourist spot. It is accessible from the Naran–Lake Saiful Muluk side and from the Batakundi–Dadar Chitta glacier, and its three summits are Malika Parbat (North Peak), Malika Parbat Cresta, and Malika Parbat (South Peak). Only twelve climbers have reached the top of the North Peak until now, while the local population considers the mountain non-climbable due to its steepness and supernatural hazards.
malika-parbat.name: Malika Parbat

batakundi.story: If you are travelling towards Babusar, Batakundi is the first town after Naran, a tourist town 15 km east of Naran in Mansehra District, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, within the Kaghan Valley. It sits along the Karakoram Highway and is a stop for jeeps, and it is the first destination on the Mansehra-Naran-Jalkhad-Chilas Road to Babusar Top, with the path further leading to Lalazar and Gilgit-Baltistan. Many people stay at hotels in Batakundi when planning their trip across Babusar Top, and it is the last town in Kaghan Valley that stays open all year, with many hotels and restaurants. Many people visit the town to see the Batakundi Waterfall.
batakundi.name: Batakundi

lulusar-dudipatsar-national-park.story: Traveller, Lulusar-Dodipat National Park lies in the Kaghan Valley in Mansehra District of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan, and was created in 2003. Its scenic Dudipatsar Lake and Lulusar Lake and peaks are in the park, and the flora includes trees, shrubs, perennials, and herbs of the Himalayan Western Himalayan subalpine conifer forests and higher elevation Western Himalayan alpine shrub and meadows ecoregions. Some of the park’s fauna includes the snow leopard, black bear, marmot, weasel, lynx, leopard, Himalayan snowcock, and the snow partridge, while its lakes and wetlands habitats are of significant ecological importance for resident fauna and migratory waterfowl. The road is accessible by cars and motorbikes, though the 2005 Kashmir earthquake in North Pakistan destroyed roads and other infrastructure and made access more difficult; since 2006 the Pakistan government has taken steps to restore tourism in the Kaghan Valley, including rebuilding and new tourism facilities and infrastructure.
lulusar-dudipatsar-national-park.name: Lulusar Lake

babusar-pass.story: For a traveller, Babusar Pass is a mountain pass at 4,173 metres at the northern end of the Kaghan Valley, connecting Khyber Pakhtunkhwa with Gilgit-Baltistan and Mansehra District with Chilas in Diamer District through the Karakoram Highway. It is the highest point in Kaghan Valley that can be easily accessed by cars, but it is also one of the most dangerous routes in Pakistan, where road accidents and brake failure in the steep landscape are reported, often due to inexperience. From mid-July until the end of September, the road north of Naran remains accessible all the way to Babusar Pass, while movement is limited during monsoon and winter, and the pass often closes due to heavy snowfall and harsh conditions. If winter closes it, travellers typically use the Karakoram Highway to access the northern regions, while the Kaghan Valley’s mountain system—including Babusar Top—flanks the right bank of the Kunhar River and contains Malika Parbat, over 17,000 feet high and the highest in the valley.
babusar-pass.name: Babusar Pass
